analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to designate PFAS 'forever chemicals' as hazardous substances and set cleanup, drinking water, and air rules.
analysis.headline: The PFAS Action Act never got a committee vote in the House and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are long-lasting 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick, waterproof, and stain-resistant products that have contaminated drinking water around the country and are linked to serious health problems. This bill would require the EPA to designate the two best-known PFAS (PFOA and PFOS) as hazardous substances under the Superfund law within 60 days, decide on the rest within five years, set national drinking water limits, list them as hazardous air pollutants, require toxicity testing, and restrict how PFAS waste is incinerated. It would also send money to water systems, schools, and territories to test for and filter out PFAS, and give manufacturers a voluntary 'PFAS-free' label program.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of people whose drinking water, wells, schools, or communities are contaminated with PFAS. The bill would speed up cleanup of polluted sites, set enforceable national drinking water limits for PFOA, PFOS, and several other PFAS, pay for water treatment systems in affected communities (prioritizing disadvantaged ones), fund testing and filters in schools and childcare centers, help territories deal with contamination, and create a website to help household well owners get their water tested. Publicly owned treatment plants would get grants to handle new discharge limits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to designate PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances under the Superfund law within 60 days, which drives cleanup of contaminated sites, and to decide within five years whether to designate all other PFAS.

Requires national primary drinking water regulations for PFOA and PFOS plus standards for PFNA, GenX, PFHxS, and PFBS, and forbids EPA from fining water systems for PFAS violations for five years after the rule.

Authorizes $500 million a year for 2024-2028 in grants to help community water systems pay for PFAS treatment technology, prioritizing disadvantaged communities, plus $100 million a year for school drinking water testing and filtration and $200 million a year to help publicly owned treatment plants meet new discharge limits.

Adds PFOA and PFOS to the Clean Air Act list of hazardous air pollutants within 180 days, requires comprehensive toxicity testing of all PFAS, bars incineration of PFAS waste except at permitted facilities that destroy the chemicals, and requires industrial users to disclose PFAS they send to treatment plants.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of PFAS and companies that discharge it (chemical makers, plastics, pulp and paper, textiles, electroplating, leather tanning, paint, and electronics plants named as 'priority industries') would bear testing, disclosure, and discharge-limit costs and Superfund cleanup liability. Waste incinerators handling PFAS would face new storage and destruction rules. Community water systems would face monitoring and treatment costs, though the bill would supply federal grant money and delay penalties for five years.

drawbacks.text: Superfund designation means anyone legally connected to a contaminated site can be pursued for cleanup costs, which can pull small businesses, water utilities, and past owners of polluted land into liability disputes, not just the original chemical makers.

New discharge limits, testing, and treatment requirements would impose real compliance costs on industrial facilities and water systems, though the bill offsets water systems' costs with $500 million a year in authorized grants and delays enforcement penalties for five years.
Many of the grant programs are only authorized, not guaranteed money; Congress would still have to appropriate the funds each year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks contamination that already affects drinking water for millions of Americans, and it puts most of the cost where the pollution came from: PFAS manufacturers and industrial dischargers, while giving affected water systems federal money and a five-year grace period before fines. The main honest concern is Superfund liability reaching parties far down the chain from the original polluters. On balance, a bill this broad would be a major win for people drinking contaminated water and a major cost for the chemical industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees from December 2023 until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, and neither committee ever voted on it, so it never reached the House floor and the Senate never saw it.

narrative.text: Representative Debbie Dingell introduced the PFAS Action Act of 2023 on December 14, 2023, with an initial list of 15 other House members including Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day it was introduced.

In the following weeks it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials and the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment; the record shows no hearings, markups, or committee votes after that.
Thirty members cosponsored the bill: 28 of 216 House Democrats and 2 of 224 House Republicans.
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and the industries that discharge or incinerate the chemicals are better off: without a law, they face no new Superfund cleanup liability, no mandatory toxicity testing, no PFAS-specific air and water discharge limits, and no incineration restrictions from this bill. Communities waiting on cleanup and safe drinking water gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from Representative Dingell (D) and Representative Fitzpatrick (R), but cosponsors were 28 of 216 House Democrats versus just 2 of 224 House Republicans, and with Republicans holding the House majority and no action ever scheduled, the support it drew was overwhelmingly Democratic.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and fluorinated chemical producers
industries.note: The bill would make PFOA and PFOS Superfund hazardous substances, force comprehensive toxicity testing on PFAS chemicals, and deem new PFAS an unreasonable risk subject to manufacture bans unless exempted for drug, device, or protective equipment research. Because these chemicals persist in drinking water and the environment, the industry's cost of avoiding cleanup and testing liability runs directly against the public's interest in safe water.

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (plastics, pulp and paper, textiles, electroplating, metal finishing, leather tanning, paint, and electronics manufacturing)
industries.note: These nine sectors are named as priority industries for Clean Water Act effluent limits on PFAS, and industrial users would have to disclose PFAS they send to treatment plants. The public's interest in clean water is the mirror of these compliance costs.

PFAS waste could only be incinerated at permitted facilities under rules requiring destruction of the chemicals and limits on air emissions, with storage standards attached. The rule targets the practice of burning PFAS waste in ways that release it into the air communities breathe.

industries.industry: Publicly owned water utilities and treatment works
industries.note: Utilities would face PFAS monitoring and treatment obligations, but the bill authorizes $500 million a year in treatment grants, a five-year penalty moratorium, and $200 million a year to help treatment plants meet discharge limits, with priority for disadvantaged communities.

industries.industry: Consumer products makers (nonstick cookware, carpets, clothing, furniture, food packaging)
industries.note: The bill creates a voluntary 'PFAS-free' label manufacturers could earn under the Safer Choice program, a marketing opportunity rather than a mandate, and it would help consumers identify products without the chemicals.
